grammar.explication: CAN sert à dire ce qu'on sait faire ou ce qu'on a le droit de faire. Il ne prend jamais de -s et il est suivi du verbe sans TO : I can swim (et pas « I can to swim »). La négation est CAN'T (cannot). À la question, CAN se met avant le sujet : Can you help me?
exemples: I can't swim but I can sing.
Can you help me please?
I can speak excellent English, good French and a little Arabic.
Pupils can learn how to play chess.

grammar.explication: MUST exprime une obligation : They must get up at seven. MUSTN'T exprime une interdiction : You mustn't laugh. Comme CAN, MUST est suivi du verbe sans TO et ne change jamais de forme. Attention à l'orthographe : mustn't, avec deux T.
exemples: Children must be polite.
They must get up at seven in the morning.
You mustn't laugh, it is not funny!
They mustn't leave school without permission.

grammar.titre: Le prétérit : les verbes réguliers en -ed
grammar.explication: Pour raconter ce qui est fini (yesterday, at Easter, ten years later), on utilise le prétérit. Les verbes réguliers prennent -ed : work → worked, watch → watched, play → played, enjoy → enjoyed. Si le verbe finit déjà par -e, on ajoute juste -d : celebrate → celebrated. La forme est la même à toutes les personnes.
exemples: Yesterday I played with my dog.
I watched a movie.
At Easter I celebrated Easter.
Yes, I enjoyed the great outdoors.

exercices.phrase: Yesterday I ___ with my dog. (play)
I ___ a movie. (watch)

I ___ a lot to get good marks. (work)
At Easter I ___ Easter. (celebrate)

exercices.question: Yes, I ___ the great outdoors.
Last week I ___ my family.

grammar.explication: Beaucoup de verbes très courants ne prennent pas -ed : il faut apprendre leur prétérit par cœur. go → went, do → did, have → had, begin → began, become → became, break → broke, be → was/were, build → built, burn → burnt. À la forme négative et à la question, on utilise DID + verbe à l'infinitif : I didn't go to church.
exemples: Yesterday I did my homework.
I went to my friends.
I had a shower.
When Luffy was still a child, bandits attacked his village.
No, I didn't go to church.

grammar.titre: THERE IS / THERE ARE (il y a)
grammar.explication: THERE IS + singulier, THERE ARE + pluriel. Négation : there isn't / there aren't. Question : Is there…? / Are there…? On répond Yes, there is. / No, there isn't.
exemples: Is there a lift in your block?
There is just one bathroom.
There are two toilets.
Next to the bed, there is a bedside table.
There aren't too many rules.

grammar.explication: En anglais, on donne d'abord les minutes, puis l'heure. On utilise PAST (après) quand l'aiguille est sur la moitié droite du cadran, et TO (jusqu'à) quand elle est sur la moitié gauche. Pour une heure pile, on dit o'clock. Le quart se dit (a) quarter et la demie half past.
exemples: It's five o'clock.
It's ten past five.
It's a quarter past six.
It's half past twelve.
It's twenty to six.

grammar.explication: En anglais, les jours et les mois s'écrivent toujours avec une majuscule. La date s'écrit July 14th, 1789 ou 14th July 1789, et se lit July the fourteenth ou the fourteenth of July. Pour lire une année, on dit les deux premiers chiffres puis les deux derniers : 1998 = nineteen ninety-eight. Depuis 2000, on peut dire twenty twenty-two ou two thousand and twenty-two.
exemples: I was born in July.
I was born on July 31st, 2012.
the fourteenth of July
nineteen ninety-eight

grammar.explication: TOO + adjectif veut dire « trop » : the water is too cold. TOO MANY + nom pluriel veut dire « trop de » : too many rules. Et TOO + adjectif + TO + verbe veut dire « trop … pour … » : it is too hot to work.
exemples: I can't swim because the water is too cold.
It is too hot to work.
There are too many rules in my opinion.
It's too good to be true.
